article_text:
Nathan Fielder’s nearly three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything , has opened to an extraordinary $15m domestic box office, the biggest opening weekend for a documentary in North America in more than 20 years.

You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, made $15m (A$21.5m, £11.2m) from only 855 screens, and had more than 2,000 sold-out screenings at the weekend, according to the production company A24. It is the biggest opening for a film playing on fewer than 1,000 screens since Borat opened to $26.5m in 2006.

It is also the biggest opening for a documentary in North America in two decades, since Fahrenheit 9/11 made nearly $24m from 868 theaters. Those numbers do not account for inflation or for concert films: Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour holds the record with a $92.8m opening weekend in 2023 when it was released in nearly 4,000 cinemas.

You Can See Everything has not opened at the international box office yet, coming out in Australia on 12 November and in the UK on 20 November.

Like other hits this year, including Backrooms and Obsession, ticket sales for You Can See Everything were driven by a largely younger audience in North America; more than 70% of the opening weekend crowd were under 35.

The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, was made in secret over three years. Fielder spent more than a month with the disgraced Theranos founder and her family, including her two young children and her partner, Billy Evans, in her final days before reporting to federal prison.

The reviews have been extremely positive, with 99% on Rotten Tomatoes and 99 on Metacritic. It also won an unprecedented 91% “definite recommend” from audiences, according to PostTrak exit polls.

You Can See Everything reportedly cost less than $7m to make and less than $10m to market.

“Everybody underestimated the movie, because on paper this is like, wait, a three-hour documentary?” said Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends for Rentrak, told Associated Press. “But [Fielder] is a huge draw, and he has a huge following on social media, and then Elizabeth Holmes is just a character that you couldn’t even make up. It’s stranger than fiction, and that’s really compelling.”

Elsewhere in the box office, Street Fighter topped the charts as expected with a $51m global opening, including $20m from international showings. The movie starring Callina Liang, Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji cost a reported $82m to make, not accounting for marketing and promotion. Audiences were 69% male.

Both Street Fighter and You Can See Everything may have contributed to Whalefall ’s relative failure at the weekend. The $60m survival thriller starring Austin Abrams and Josh Brolin made $8m from 3,065 locations in the US and Canada, despite being better reviewed than Street Fighter. With $9.5m from international showings, the Disney release had a total $17.5m global launch.

Whalefall opened in fourth place, behind the Jessica Chastain horror Other Mommy, which took $8.4m domestically in its second weekend, adding to its $78.7m global total.

Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary Musk also expanded to 472 screens in the US and Canada, making $306,702. The film, which runs for nearly four hours, has faced problems advertising on major social media platforms including X, which Musk owns, and TikTok, according to its distributor, Bleecker Street, which said that at the weekend TikTok had permanently suspended the film’s ad account.

Netflix also shared ticket sales for the first time for the queer Spanish epic La Bola Negra, which made $277,500 from four locations at the weekend. The streamer has not historically reported box office for its theatrical releases but this film is breaking new ground as it is being positioned as a possible best picture contender. It will be in theatres for 47 days before it will be available to watch on Netflix.

According to Rentrak, the weekend overall generated about $101.6m in ticket sales, up 45% from the same weekend last year. The year to date stands at $8.2bn, which is up almost 20% from 2025.

– Associated Press contributed to this report

架空の画家に擬態する現代美術家と戦後の前衛美術。小川哲も参加

東京・中村橋の 練馬区立美術館 で、企画展 「ユアサエボシと戦後アヴァンギャルドの変身寓話集」 が開催されている。会期は12月27日まで。担当は同館の 木下紗耶子 学芸員。

本展は、「変身」をキーワードに、現代美術家の ユアサエボシ の新作を含む絵画群と、戦後に前衛美術を追求した 池田龍雄（1928～2020）、高山良策（1917～1982）、中村宏（1932～2026） の代表作など計約100点を展示。ユアサは1983年千葉県生まれ。「大正生まれの架空の三流画家・ユアサヱボシ」という設定で絵画制作に取り組み、自身を「擬態派」と呼ぶ。戦後と現代を往還する試みは高く評価され、 金沢21世紀美術館 や 東京都現代美術館 などに作品が収蔵されている。

本展を企画した意図を木下は次のように話す。

「ユアサさんの作品は、古い大衆文化やキッチュな要素も含む異質なモチーフ同士が緊張感を持って組み立てられ、絵画として非常に面白い。またユアサさんが変身して絵画を制作するユアサヱボシ（以下ヱボシ）は、当館の重要な所蔵作家である池田や高山、中村と設定のうえで同時代の画家でもある。ふたつを接続することで、戦後日本の前衛美術における『変身』モチーフの広がりと多様性を探るとともに、過去に対する鑑賞者の想像力を喚起できればと思う」

本展には、2023年に直木賞を受賞した小説家の 小川哲（1986～） も参加し、架空の物故詩人になりきって「ヱボシ」に影響を与えたとされる詩を書き、会場で発表。ユアサが絵画とともに年譜を発表してきた「ヱボシ」の生涯の物語に、新たなエピソードが加わるかたちとなった。

戦争の時代を生き、アメリカ文化に影響を受けた「ユアサヱボシ」

同館2階から始まる本展は、第1章ではユアサの絵画世界にフォーカス。新聞や雑誌、インターネット上で採集したイメージを組み合わせて絵画を制作するユアサは、戦後の日本美術に多大な影響を与えたシュルレアリスムに興味を持ち、その時代を生きた「ヱボシ」が描いた設定で2017年から作品の発表を始めた。本章には、初期作から新作までの22点が、作品に見られる特徴的な要素である「アメリカ文化」「戦争」などに分けられて並ぶ。

冒頭の《女性工員No.6》は、機械化された空間にアメリカン・コミック調の女性や巨大なベーコン、立ち上る黒煙が描かれ、不吉な予感が漂う。異質なイメージ同士を出合わせるシュルレアリスムの代表的手法「デペイズマン」を用いた初期の代表作だ。

ユアサが作成した年譜（もちろん虚構）によると、「ヱボシ」は1924年に生まれ、看板屋の職に就きながら福沢一郎の絵画研究所で学び、戦後はアメリカ文化の影響を受けて渡米。2年間の滞米中は岡田謙三の勧めで抽象画を描き始めたといい、その作品も会場に展示されている。日本におけるシュルレアリスム導入の立役者だった福沢も戦後アメリカに渡った岡田も実在した画家であり、鑑賞者は「偽」と「真」を行き来して想像も働かせながら作品を見ることになる。

徴兵検査で不合格となり、戦地に行かなかった設定の「ヱボシ」。会場には「戦争」にまつわる作品も並び、異国の熱帯林といった「戦争記録画」に似た戦場風景が描かれるが、現実の悲惨さはなく寓話感が先立つ。看板屋だった前歴がうかがえる平坦な絵肌とくっきりとした輪郭、漫画由来の「のらくろ」や明るい子供などのイメージが、童話めいた雰囲気を画面に演出している。

架空の詩人が満州国で書いた詩、「変容」した人物像

本展のために制作された新作《傀儡（くぐつ）の王》は、「変身」に込めた寓意が顕著な作品だ。「ヱボシ」が戦後に描いたと位置づけられ、鞭を手にした騎手は傀儡国家・満州国を建国した日本、王冠を被った大蛇は皇帝溥儀を諧謔的に表しているそうだ。本作に影響を与えたという触れ込みで架空の詩人が満州国で書いたとされる詩（実際の作者は小川哲）も併せて展示され、フィクションをさらに強化している。満州の架空の都市を舞台にした小説『地図と拳』を著した小川とユアサによる、たくらみに満ちたコラボレーションと言えるだろう。

頭部をすげ替えて、人物の属性や社会的身分を変容させた絵画も多い。シュルレアリスムやアメリカ文化、日本のルポルタージュ絵画の影響を受けた作品を展開したものの、画家として成功しないまま世を去った「ヱボシ」。辛辣な表現は、彼と同じように時代に翻弄された多くの人々の眼差しが重なるようであり、同時にわずかな改変で揺らぐ権威の危うさや滑稽さも感じさせる。

高山良策、池田龍雄、中村宏の「変身」の表現

続く第2章では、架空の「ヱボシ」と活動期がオーバーラップする高山良策、池田龍雄、中村宏の同館所蔵の作品を紹介。戦後に前衛美術を志した3人が、日本の政治や社会の激変と不条理、戦争の記憶と向き合い、それぞれの視点から生み出した「変身」の表現を概観する。

高山は、戦前は福沢一郎の研究所に通い、戦後は左翼的な美術団体の前衛美術会を舞台に活動するなど、「ヱボシ」と共通項が多い。多様な素材を用いた絵画を制作し、特撮テレビ番組『ウルトラマン』の怪獣の着ぐるみの制作を担ったことでも知られる。展示されている絵画とドローイングは、生命があるように見える機械や擬人化された動植物、仮面を思わせる顔の造形が特徴的だ。

特攻隊員として終戦を迎えた池田は、画家を志して上京し、様々な文化人と交流して岡本太郎らのアヴァンギャルド芸術運動に加わった。ペン画によるルポルタージュ絵画で注目され、50年代半ばに始めた「化物の系譜」シリーズでは人間や動物がモノと合体したようなキメラ的な生き物を描いた。社会の現実や人間の内奥に向けた批評的な眼差しは、この時期の油彩画にも見て取れる。

終戦時12歳だった中村は、大学在学中に学生運動に飛び込み、社会的出来事に取材するルポルタージュ絵画運動に取り組んだ。60年代以降、繰り返し描いたモチーフがセーラー服の女学生だ。生家は女学校を経営し、幼少期から女学生は身近な存在だったという。作品では機械と合成された姿や巨大な一つ目の怪物めいた存在に描かれ、中村のアンビバレントな感情をうかがわせる。

「変身広場」に集う、「虚」と「実」の戦後絵画

「変身広場」と題する本展のラストは、他館からの借用作品も交えて1階の展示室で展開する。「子ども」「ばけもの」「仮面」のテーマ別に、ユアサと第2章の3人、他の画家たちによる「変身絵画」を混ぜて展示。「フェイク」と「リアル」の戦後絵画を通して、おもに50年代の前衛美術における人間像の変容や身体表現の変質、政治・社会の矛盾を突く寓話的表現を見つめる試みだ。

戦前にパリで抽象芸術やシュルレアリスム運動に関わり、戦時中は従軍し、戦後日本でアヴァンギャルド芸術運動を展開した岡本太郎（1911～96）。1954年の作品《遊ぶ子》は、動き回る姿が正体の見えない流動的な形状に描かれ、子供のパワーともろさを感じさせる。ろうけつ染めによる絵画を手がけた芥川（間所）紗織（1924～1966）の《女Ⅲ》は、大胆にデフォルメした顔が仮面を思わせ、大きく開いた口は叫ぶように見える。ちなみにユアサが擬態する「ヱボシ」は芥川と同年の生まれに設定されており、ふたりは接点があったかも、などと想像するのも楽しい。

「変身広場」の展示作のなかでユアサがとくに惹かれると言うのは、古沢岩美（1912～2000）の《日本の70年（コウモリ・男の顔）》。日本列島の図の上に、翼を広げるコウモリや牙をむく蛇を描き、新聞の見出しや写真を散りばめた晩期の大作だ。「普段あまり見る機会がない、こうした謎めいて面白い作品を、本展を機に多くの人に見てもらえるとうれしい」と話す。

敗戦を境に政治、社会の体制と価値観が覆るなか、新しい表現が芽吹いた戦後の日本。ユアサが「ヱボシ」を生み出した背景には、この時代に対する強い関心があったという。「憧れの澁澤龍彦や三島由紀夫と同時代に生きて活躍したかった。その葛藤を、ヱボシを設定することで解消できた」と振り返る。

いっぽうで、制作の際はまず先に「描きたいビジュアル」があり、作品の意味や文脈は後付けだと説明する。「それでいて『歴史の穴』みたいな所に嵌ることがよくある。そういう偶然をヱボシの物語を作るうえで僕は利用している。時代は違っても、人間が描きたいものはさほど変わらないということかもしれない」

虚構が史実に近づき、史実が虚構を補強する。「フェイク」と「リアル」が入れ子状になった本展は、現代にも通じる「変身」の多義性をひもときながら、過去との向き合い方を問いかけている。

A View From the Easel: Leslie Lewis Sigler

“The light and studio interior are literally reflected in my work.”

Welcome to the 363rd installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Leslie Lewis Sigler paints spoons and their trick-mirror images in the changing California light.

Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form ! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

Leslie Lewis Sigler , Soquel, California

How long have you been working in this space?

Nine months. We built the studio in our backyard last year. I had a studio in our garage prior to moving into this space.

UPDATED: In the wake of a four-hour long flight ground stop, Hollywood can still expect a weekend of disruptions after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the shutdown Friday evening. Travel plans were thrown into question for talent, executives and buyers headed to and from Los Angeles and New York during one of the busiest stretches on the industry calendar.

The FAA says it grounded flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It marks the most extensive disruption to air travel in the U.S. since the federal government mandated a total shutdown of all activity after the 9/11 attacks in September 2001. Some flights resumed immediately, but hundreds of others were canceled while travelers scrambled to make new plans.

Isabelle Huppert Vampire Film ‘The Blood Countess’ Was Cut Against Director’s Wishes, Ulrike Ottinger Tells Tokyo Event

From the Motion Picture Academy’s Governors Awards to an array of premieres, screenings, concerts, among myriad other events, Hollywood’s plans as film award season kicks in to high gear were thrown into total disarray. The same is true for innumerable professional and college football and basketball games. CNN estimated that some 1.5 million travelers were left stranded in airports, on runways or on trips that inevitably had to be extended amid the ground stop.

The cause is not yet clear, but an FAA spokesperson says a communications problem affected the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle flights moving across the country. Preliminary reports indicate it is not a cyberattack, according to law enforcement officials and media outlets. The rare ground stop, which was announced just after 1 p.m. PT, led to more than 7,800 flights across the U.S. being delayed by Friday evening, according to the air travel tracking service FlightAware.

article_text:
Shows

Up Close: Sasha Gordon’s Portrait of Obsession

SASHA GORDON ’s

Hard Candies , 2026. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner, New York.

Nocturnal David Zwirner Hong Kong Sep 23 – Nov 14, 2026

Sasha Gordon’s sitter has a center part that is worryingly wide; I fret over it with the same scrutiny I give my own every morning. The unsettling fissure zigzags down her scalp, perhaps styled to soften the seam a straighter course would expose. The delicate strands, delineated with a finesse as cruel as it is heartbreakingly tender, gather into ebony banks fringing an emerald river of skin.

The face, this time, is not Gordon’s. Departing from the proliferating selves of her usual output, she depicts an anonymous friend in Hard Candies (2026), included in the group exhibition “Nocturnal” curated by Matthew Brown at David Zwirner Hong Kong. The gallery is on my way home, and across several visits my fixation has followed the same route: first the sparse roots, then the stray wisps that lead down to vitreous auburn pupils, themselves fixed on a glass paperweight poised gingerly in her hands.

SASHA GORDON ,

Hard Candies , 2026. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner, New York.

The talisman, held aloft with a reverence bordering on supplication, is an heirloom from Gordon’s grandmother. Here the artist’s technical virtuosity verges on ostentation: fungal growths and botanical forms swell and flourish in a miniature terrarium, their warping contours and kindling colors aflare in glancing light.

So much is available to the eye, yet nothing yields. A sumptuous white mohair crewneck solicits yet forbids touch, conveying at once a soft vulnerability and something feral, prickly. Behind her, misty lavender tiles suggest a bathroom humid with steam. These diffuse textures hush the edges of the picture, allowing for a sharp convergence of focus where the sitter’s attention and ours meet. And what we most obsess over is the most out of reach: an enclosed, precarious world sealed against access.

That withholding follows a period of giving too much of herself. Having made her own likeness so central to her work, Gordon is reconsidering the terms of that intimacy. “I think I have been very earnest. In the past year I started to feel quite vulnerable,” she tells me. “Like I’ve been a little too generous.”

The conspicuous hair part carries a trace of that openness. She recalls an earlier painting about trichotillomania, a work made with a candor she now hesitates to repeat. The detail in this work is something of a private joke—“an homage to that version of myself,” she explains.

Details of SASHA GORDON ’s Hard Candies , 2026. Courtesy the artist and David Zwirner, New York.

Here the face belongs to someone else, but the psychological charge has not diminished. “I think the figure is actually not what’s the most important in this piece. It’s the textures that add up to the figure. I am interested in psychological spaces and in creating spaces of tension, and here I was thinking about how I could express that not through a face or a portrait, but an object.”

Her expression inscrutable, the sitter’s absorption admits no audience. And yet Hard Candies arrests us precisely through this spectacle of attention we cannot enter: the figure’s gaze could be appreciation, grief, even hatred, or a kind of burning, searching, hope. In conversation I remark that the object feels to me like a crystal ball, teasing a future in its depths. “It is more than a crystal ball or a paperweight,” Gordon corrects me. “It could be like a loved one, or a memory.”

In portraying obsession, the painting also induces it, the paperweight a stand-in for all that we cannot bear to relinquish. But even the fiercest vigilance cannot forestall loss, nor scrutiny keep hair from thinning. A hard candy invites us to hold it gently on the tongue, resisting the impulse to bite; yet even the tenderest restraint does not stop it dissolving.

Michele Chan is managing editor at ArtAsiaPacific.

横浜・山下ふ頭のイマーシブ・ミュージアム 「THE MOVEUM YOKOHAMA by TOYOTA GROUP」 が、10月24日にリニューアルオープン。新コンテンツとして、 クロード・モネ と日本の浮世絵のつながりに着目したシアタープログラム 「印象派モネと浮世絵 ［モネを魅了した、日本の美］」 がスタートする。映像や音楽、空間演出を通して、印象派と浮世絵が交差する芸術の世界に没入できる。会期は2027年3月31日まで。

新プログラムでは、 葛飾北斎 や 歌川広重 、 喜多川歌麿 らが生み出した浮世絵の表現と、モネの作品とのつながりを探る。独自の構図や自然のとらえ方など、日本美術から影響を受けた西洋の芸術家たち。なかでもモネは熱心な浮世絵の収集家として知られ、40年以上を過ごしたジヴェルニーの邸宅にも多くの作品を飾っていた。

会場では、モネや印象派画家たちの作品を大規模な映像として空間全体に投影し、音楽や建築、音響と融合させる。プログラムは「プロローグ 日の出」から始まり、「印象派と近代都市パリ」「パリから海へ：光をもとめて」「自然のなかへ」「ジャポニスム」「浮世絵：江戸の美と新たな視覚表現」「睡蓮：移ろう光、はてしない風景」の6章を経て、「エピローグ 日没、光と影」で締めくくられる。光や季節の移ろいを追い続けたモネのまなざしと、浮世絵がもたらした革新的な視覚表現を、作品を鑑賞するだけでなく、その世界に身を置きながら味わえる。

メインシアターの奥には、モネが晩年まで暮らしたジヴェルニーの邸宅に着想を得た「モネのダイニングルーム」も登場。北斎や広重、歌麿らの浮世絵が飾られていた空間をイメージし、モネの日常と日本美術とのつながりを感じられる世界観を作り出す。浮世絵の歴史や表現、作品を支えた職人の技を紹介する「浮世絵ギャラリー」も併設される。

そのほか、俳優・ 山口智子 のライフワークであり、プロデューサーを務めるプロジェクト「LISTEN.」から、イマーシブアートと融合したシリーズ「ONE MOMENT」の新作「WHITE NIGHT 白夜」を上映。10年をかけて約26ヶ国を巡り、未来へ残したい「音」を映像に収めてきた同プロジェクト。今回の新作では、北の大地に息づく音や自然の営みを、映像と音楽で体験できる。また、「トヨタ夢のクルマアートコンテスト」の入賞作品を没入型映像として上映する企画も実施される。

会場の山下ふ頭エントランスから展示空間までは、トヨタのモビリティ「e-Palette（イーパレット）」が運行。今回のリニューアルでは自動運転の実証も予定している。アートとテクノロジーが融合する新たな文化体験の場として、その進化にも注目したい。

On this week’s Podcast, Boots Riley joins to discuss his new film, I Love Boosters . The director of 2018’s Sorry to Bother You and the 2023 streaming series I’m a Virgo has returned with a movie that provides a new, invigorating riff on the theme that runs through all his work: the destruction of capitalism by an organized working class. I Love Boosters , which opens in theaters later this month, is a kaleidoscopic joyride that features professional shoplifters, lurking demons, a Marxist teleportation device, and more, all anchored by a cast par excellence : Keke Palmer in the lead, with Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige, Demi Moore, Eiza González, Will Poulter, Don Cheadle, and LaKeith Stanfield making up a pitch-perfect ensemble.

Film Comment Editor Devika Girish had a long conversation with Boots about everything from how he got into fashion when he was depressed to why it’s important for him to make movies that show that the left can win.

article_text:
Art Review

The Artist Who Dined Among Lions

California performance artist Bonnie Ora Sherk was a cultural trickster and proactive spoiler in the business of everyday life.

Hyperallergic )

SANTA BARBARA — People didn’t always live in cities. It became more of the norm as asphalt and concrete covered dirt, and highways and overpasses became the infrastructure for commuting and delivering food and supplies. Bonnie Ora Sherk (1945–2021) spent four decades as an artist, landscape designer, and educator challenging the assumptions that underpin city life. Through her creative projects, Sherk consistently proposed new models of social relations. The retrospective Life Frames since 1970 at the University of California, Santa Barbara’s Museum of Art, Design, and Architecture, is a well-designed, if modest, exhibition that highlights many of her interventions, from performances to interactive engagements, as documented in drawings, posters, photographs, and moving images.

Sherk began as a cultural trickster, like many conceptually based artists from the late 1950s onward, often acting as both observer and observed — and proactive spoiler — in the business of everyday life. After studying with Fluxus artists Robert Watts and Mel Henderson, Sherk applied a post-Dadaist performance sensibility to visionary yet practical rethinking of human priorities, promoting mindful encounters with other living creatures.

Because much of the exhibition is documentary, the aesthetics are somewhat limited, with occasional visual pleasures. Set in mundane outdoor locations in San Francisco, Sherk’s series Sitting Still (1970) — in which the artist places herself in ordinary chairs amid daily urban life — is presented in the exhibition through projections of large-scale Kodachrome photographs. Nearby, a black-and-white film transferred to video documents “ Public Lunch ” (1971), projecting Sherk caged in the San Francisco Zoo’s Lion House next to big cats in a neighboring lockup, as visitors gawked while both cats and the artist paced, napped, and were fed.

Around the same time, she began creating pop-up spaces around the city under the umbrella title Portable Parks I-III (1970). Set above and below active highway overpasses or in busy downtown alleyways, these public "parks" held livestock and cultivated plants. This culminated in an early peak with Crossroads Community (aka The Farm) (1974–80), where Sherk catalyzed social possibilities through sustained interactions and shared knowledge about animal husbandry and urban homesteading, along with an array of musical and experimental performances by numerous artists.

Resonant with diverse back-to-the-land initiatives in the 1960s and '70s — and a feminist contrast to Land Art’s distant locations and monumentality — Sherk’s divergent vision insisted on staying with the city, offering alternatives to how urban spaces were organized and focusing on neglected, under-resourced communities. These interventions opened the door to a swirling proliferation of anarchistic community access and cultural production, while pushing the frame of what might be considered conceptual art practice. Much recurrent activity at The Farm emerged under the rubric “T.R.E.A.T.” for “The Raw Egg Animal Theater” – a typical bit of serious whimsy on Sherk’s part that named an open-ended interactive staging ground for plants, humans and other animals. Over the years, thousands participated in programs at The Farm, accessing ideas, information, and other living creatures they would not otherwise have encountered.

There are many aspects about both Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti that stand out. There’s the breadth of work both actors have turned in over the course of their decades-long careers — plus the Oscar wins, nominations, and other accolades — but the one that most thrilled their “ The Debut ” writer/director Jesse Eisenberg was how quickly they could nail a take.

“Oh, my God. Paul and Julianne, I feel like I have trouble describing this to people who don’t make movies every day, because it’s so unusual. But normally, when you’re making a movie, especially the people who are the leads, they take five or six takes, meaning you do the scene five or six times before they become comfortable with their prop and now their lines. And now they realize that the light’s going to be there. And you very rarely, if never, ever find two actors who on their first takes are perfect with their performance, with props, with lines,” said the recently Oscar-nominated “A Real Pain” filmmaker while speaking to the audience at the Middleburg Film Festival, where “The Debut” served as the opening night film .

Eisenberg happened to be seated next to Moore as he was extolling on the skill of both her and her co-star (who unfortunately was out sick). “With every moment, what you’re seeing in this movie is the first and second take of the two lead performers to the point, where the first two days we had scheduled on the schedule — we were trying for eight days of musical numbers, big ensemble — we shot them in one day,” he said.

The filmmaker (and newly minted songwriter) previously spoke to IndieWire, explaining that although “ The Debut ” has actors of Moore and Giamatti’s caliber, it was still an independent film at the end of the day. “This is a small budget movie. [Nobody got paid oodles of money],” he said. “When you have actors like this, they’re great. When they were good, we would go to the next scene.” And the budget remains more than stable.

At Middleburg, Eisenberg again said that the reason he was comfortable making “The Debut” that way, shooting one or two takes of each scene of the humorous movie musical hybrid, “is all because they were perfect. And it’s like you see the first take and you’re like, ‘We can do it again, but we would waste film? It’s perfect.’ So it was all that.”

article_text:
Korean filmmaker Lee Hwan-kyung , director of “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” has assembled an Indonesian ensemble led by Vino G. Bastian , Pevita Pearce, Faradina Mufti and Indra Jegel for “ Gasigogi ,” a father-son drama now in production with Falcon Pictures.

The film follows Jiwa, a father who sacrifices everything in a fight to save Juna, his son, who has blood cancer. Bastian plays the lead, with Pearce as co-lead and Mufti as Chitra. Falcon Pictures unveiled the cast together with Hwantasy Entertainment.

Bastian starred in the Indonesian remake of “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” while Pearce is known for “5 cm” and Mufti for “Impetigore.” The supporting cast includes Altaaf Akavi (“Tunggu Aku Sukses Nanti”), Indro Warkop (“Miracle in Cell No. 7”), Dea Panendra (“Marlina the Murderer in Four Acts”), Sadana Agung (“Agak Laen”), Irma Novita Rihi (“Women From Rote Island”), Luisa Adreena (“Na Willa”), Pritt Timothy (“Ayah, Aku Mau Cerita”), Verdi Solaiman (“The Raid”) and Kiki Narendra (“Ghost in the Cell”).

Popular on Variety

The working title takes its inspiration from the stickleback fish. The male of the species remains alone with the eggs and fights off predators until his body gives out, at which point his flesh becomes the hatchlings’ first food. Lee uses the image as a metaphor for fatherhood and the sacrifices parents make for their children.

The project marks Lee’s return to directing following the success of the Indonesian version of his earlier phenomenon, and he has called it the most emotionally taxing film he has taken on. He made “Miracle in Cell No. 7” as a gift for his daughter. “Gasigogi” is dedicated to his son.

By shooting in Indonesia, Lee wants to draw on the country’s strong attachment to family, faith and community. He said the film is an original work rather than a transplant of Korean feeling, one that “breathes with Indonesian lungs.”

“Just as a father gives everything to his child, I want to pour everything I have into creating a precious gift for this family,” Lee said. “The name of that gift is ‘Gasigogi.’ The goal is simple: I want to create a film so honest and resonant that when the credits roll, the first thing the audience wants to do is call their father.”

“To be trusted with a story of this magnitude is both an incredible honor and a tremendous emotional challenge,” Bastian added. “Director Lee has crafted a raw, devastating, and beautiful narrative about what a father will endure for his child.”

Mufti said she was grateful to Falcon and Lee for entrusting her with Chitra. “As a mother myself, this story feels very close to my heart,” she said. “It reminds me that love isn’t always expressed through words, but often through the things we do and the sacrifices we make for our children.”

Falcon producer Frederica added, “The unparalleled dedication of our brilliant cast and crew, combined with Director Lee’s masterful storytelling, makes ‘Gasigogi’ a truly special project. We believe this film will leave a lasting, emotional legacy for Indonesian cinema and audiences everywhere.”

article_text:
Richard Riehle , known for playing Tom Smykowski in “Office Space” and many other character actor roles, died of natural causes Oct. 15 in Los Angeles, Variety has confirmed. He was 78.

His reps shared in a statement, “A remarkable actor whose career in theater, film, and television spanned nearly five decades and more than 400 projects, Richard leaves behind an extraordinary legacy. Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity. Our industry has lost an exceptional talent, and our community has lost a truly wonderful man.”

Riehle was born in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin, on May 12, 1948. He attended the University of Notre Dame before receiving a masters from University of Minnesota. He began acting at the Meadow Brook Theatre in Rochester, Michigan, and was doing regional theatre in the Pacific Northwest when he appeared in the John Wayne film “Rooster Cogburn.”

As Tom in “Office Space,” Riehle played the product manager who was laid off from Initech, survived a hit-and-run accident and landed a massive financial settlement that allowed him to follow his dreams and build his prototype “Jump to Conclusions” mat.

On TV, he portrayed Walt Finnerty on “Grounded for Life.” He had multiple appearances across the “Star Trek” franchise, including the role of Batai in “The Next Generation” episode “The Inner Light.” He also had guest roles in shows like “NCIS,” “The Middle” and “The West Wing.”

Riehle appeared in over 400 films, television shows and other projects. His other roles include the ranch hand Carlson in “Of Mice and Men,” the guard who allowed Harrison Ford to escape custody in “The Fugitive,” Principal Beasely in the Pauly Shore comedy “Jury Duty,” and parts in “Executive Decision,” “Mercury Rising,” “Deuce Bigalow: Male Gigolo,” “Wedding Crashers,” “Bridesmaids” and many more. Across his career and many roles, Riehle has portrayed Santa Claus in eight different projects, including five films, two television shows, and a television movie.

He is survived by his wife, Jane Latham, and their four children.

article_text:
GIJÓN, Spain — Taking place in northern Spain under two monhs after the San Sebastián International Film Festival and linked to it by the Cross Roads initiative, the 64th Gijón International Film Festival (FICX) lineup stacks many of the year’s most talked-about features from international festivals such as Cannes, Berlin, Venice and Sundance.

At the same time, running Nov. 13-20, the festival serves as a springboard for new local talent into the international arena, which the festival has championed for decades.

Related Stories

‘The Remarried Empress’ Becomes Most-Viewed Local Original Premiere Ever on Disney+ and Hulu

The Game Awards Adds Disney+ to Livestream Lineup

FICX’s influence extends to the new Spanish talent currently rising with recognition: Oliver Laxe (“Sirât”), Jonás Trueba (“The Other Way Around”) and Carla Simon (“Alcarràs”) are closely linked with Gijón. Both Laxe and Trueba showcased their first works at the festival and have built long careers since their early FICX selections. Simón had her very own first retrospective at Gijón.

The Gijón Festival has a long standing tradition of mixing rising and established talent, top-tier international and regional voice rubbing shoulders, becoming a beacon for emerging talent.

This year’s edition opened Nov. 13 with James Gray’s “ Paper Tiger ,” screening in Gijón’s main Albar section. Gray’s previous feature, “Armageddon Time,” also opened the 2022 Gijón festival.

Closing the festival on Nov. 20 is Peter Farrelly’s “ I Play Rocky ,” described by Variety’s Owen Gleiberman as “a cleverly crafted crowd-pleaser, all designed to tap into the love of ‘Rocky’ that has never gone away.”

“On one side we bring big names from the international industry, as we’ve done in previous editions,” explained FICX director Alejandro Díaz Castaño. “We also bring top-Spanish talent and well-established filmmakers such as Albert Serra (“Sixteen Moments of My Life”) or Hal Hartley (“Where To Land”).

Albar, the festival’s main competition, includes 21 features aiming for the top prize. Albar’s selection includes Cannes Directors’ Fortnight winner Clio Barnard’s “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning,” Grant Lee’s Berlin Silver Bear winner “Everybody Digs Bill Evans” and Visar Morina’s “Shame and Money,” winner of the World Cinema Dramatic Grand Jury prize at Sundance.

“I think we ended up having many unclassifiable features, which do not fully fit into more structured selections because of their strong auteurist component,” explained Díaz Castaño. “Here at Gijón, we are really into that mix of genres, those hybrids that tend to live on the margins.”

Among the Albar titles is Valeska Grisebach’s Cannes Jury Prize winner “The Dreamed Adventure.” No stranger to either the city or the festival, Grisebach’s previous work “Longing” took the festival’s best feature prize back in 2006.

Hong Sang-soo, a Gijón favorite who has won FICX best feature prize three times, arrives at this edition’s Albar with “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” which scooped the best director prize at Locarno.

Radu Jude, another Gijón’s regular who scored Albar’s top prize in 2023 with “Do Not Expect Too Much From the End of the World,” returns with “The Diary of a Chambermaid,” which premiered at Cannes Directors’ Fortnight.

“We are also lucky to have some regular, highly talented attendees from both the local and international landscape, such as Lisandro Alonso (“Eureka”), Albert Serra, Radu Jude and Hong Sangsoo,” added Díaz Castaño.

László Nemes’ “Moulin,” Jeanne Herry’s “Garance” and Angela Schanelec’s “My Wife Cries” round out a competition that includes Mads Mengel’s Karlovy Vary winner “The Guest.”

Nicolas Pariser’s Venice contender “One Minute to Midnight” will screen out of competition. “The Italian coda is sweet, allowing Pariser to redeem the concept of love from the cynicism of a world wary of romance,” wrote Variety’s Jay Weissberg .

Retueyos, focusing on directors promoting their second or third feature, opens with Pierre Le Gall’s “Flesh and Fuel,” winner of Cannes’ Queer Palme Révélation prize. It also includes Venice Orizzonti winner Ann Sirot and Raphaël Balboni’s “Un détour par Diane.”

The festival’s Premiere section brings international features to Spain for their premieres. It has expanded to 16 titles. Among attending filmmakers is Gregg Araki , who returns to the festival with Sundance title “ I Want Your Sex ,” starring Cooper Hoffman and Olivia Wilde. Araki first visited Gijón in 1996, presenting three of his early works, “The Living End,” “Totally F***ed Up” and “The Doom Generation.” He was also the subject of a 1999 FICX retrospective.

Other Spain premieres take in Céline Sciamma’s cinematic essay “Tutti Frutti”; Jia Zhangke’s Cannes title “Torino Shadow”; Cédric Kahn’s Venice screener “A Place to Heal”; Ulrike Ottinger’s vampire fantasy “The Blood Countess,” starring Isabelle Huppert; and Mohammad Rasoulof’s 39-minute “Sense of Water.”

Sangsoo will also be on hand for Gijón presentation of “The Day She Returns,” which is set to open in U.S. theaters next month.

Thanks to the festival’s relation with its audience, its success on ticket sales and its relentless pursuit of partners and collaborations, five San Sebastián Festival titles arrive at Gijón as part of the festival’s Cross Roads initiative. The list includes Fred Cavayé’s “Les Mirsérables,” Jesse Steinberg’s “The Debut” and Javier Ruiz Caldera’s “5 More Minutes.”

Gijón continues to support talent, collaborating with the Asturias Paraiso Natural Film Commision on FICX Pro, its industry wing and on the Semilleru project development lab, which provide opportunities for local Asturian and Spanish professionals.

“What we aim to do is to bring the city together and push together and rally support behind the festival, working hard with local and regional entities, local government, and private initiatives and citizens. The festival becomes like a hub where everyone tunes in to connect and where everyone can find their place,” added Diaz Castaño.

article_text:
Al Maschio Angioino di Napoli , fino al 25 ottobre 2026, la mostra 80 Repubblica: Memorie di donne, fotografie e racconti di ottant’anni di democrazia propone un viaggio nella memoria attraverso fotografie, documenti e opere pittoriche, assumendo come filo conduttore la figura femminile e il suo ruolo nella storia democratica del Paese. Il percorso mette in relazione le vicende personali con alcuni passaggi centrali della nascita della Repubblica, a partire dal diritto di voto conquistato dalle donne.

In una delle fotografie in esposizione di Gabriele Colafranceschi si distinguono le mani giunte di una donna anziana accanto a un rosario, immagine che restituisce una dimensione intima e quotidiana del ricordo. Accanto ai ritratti ai sali d’argento trovano spazio anche Le Voci della Democrazia , testimonianze che riportano alla luce esperienze e ricordi legati a quella fase storica. Una delle protagoniste racconta, per esempio, i momenti salienti del Referendum. A completare il percorso, gli affreschi di donne di Aerma Polani e le ricerche di Ivano Nobile e del professor Enzo Palumbo .

Negli spazi del Castello, l’imponenza delle pietre medievali diventa un guscio naturale per accogliere scatti e video così intimi, come racconta la curatrice della mostra, Rosanna Menduni De Rossi : «In realtà la comunione tra questi due fattori diametralmente opposti è stata fondamentale. L’aspetto monumentale di queste sale è colonna portante dello sguardo intimo dell’artista su un tema altrettanto imponente: quello del tempo che scorre, tra le mura medievali del castello come tra i volti pieni di vita di queste donne».

A spiegare il senso profondo del progetto e le varie tappe, dal lavoro con le donne che hanno testimoniato quella storia alla scelta del linguaggio analogico, è la voce di Gabriele Colafranceschi, che ha contribuito alla mostra con fotografie e video: «Il 2 giugno 1946 non solo si è votato per il referendum, ma è stato anche l’anno in cui le donne hanno votato per la prima volta a livello nazionale. Attraverso le “madri” della nostra repubblica, donne nate in concomitanza dei suoi albori, ho voluto ridare luce alle loro preziose testimonianze, legate all’aria di cambiamento che si respirava in quel periodo e alla rivoluzione di genere che ha iniziato a concretizzarsi soprattutto in quegli anni, grazie al significativo contributo di ognuna.

Donna e democrazia sono entrambe custodi della vita. Lavorando a queste immagini ho sentito prima di tutto una profonda curiosità verso la memoria di un tempo che non ho vissuto; l’unico dovere per il quale mi sono sentito responsabile è stato quello di essere fedele nel raccontare chi avevo davanti, ed onesto, per permettere a chi guarda di provare quello che ho provato io.

Il mio amore per la fotografia nasce nel momento in cui ho capito che grazie alle immagini posso esprimere qualcosa che a parole non sarei capace: proprio per questa mia profonda necessità, il mezzo è sempre in secondo piano e la fotocamera utilizzata per questo progetto è un segreto che mantengo per me. Durante lo scatto sento di essere al posto giusto, sempre. La fotografia più rappresentativa è il ritratto delle mani di una delle donne intervistate, dove nel processo di stampa in camera oscura ho impressionato un rosario: mi riporta con il pensiero al ricordo di una persona che non appartiene più alla mia vita».

article_text:
It looks as if those Netflix cuts and trims are not over just yet.

Netflix’s head of film , Dan Lin , has been let go from the gig after less than three years at the streamer, a source with knowledge of his exit told IndieWire. Lin is the latest big name cut, joining the firing of chief content officer Bela Bajaria last week and a large-scale set of layoffs that have so far impacted about 1,000 Netflix employees. The layoffs also impacted high-ranking members of Lin’s team, including Doug Belgrad and indie film head Sheroum Kim.

Variety adds via multiple sources that Lin was let go at the start of the weekend and will address his teams throughout the day Monday. It’s unclear who will replace Lin, and rumors have abounded that ousted Warner Bros. film chiefs Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy could be in the running, but Netflix is clearly in the midst of a major restructuring that goes beyond layoffs. Lauded film and TV executive Peter Rice has already been tapped to replace Bajaria.

“It’s been a great privilege to lead this incredible team and work with amazing filmmakers and talent to bring their movies to the world. Thank you to Ted, Greg and Bela for the opportunity,” Lin said in a brief statement.

“I started working with Dan well before he joined us in 2024 and his strength as a producer was always clear,” Ted Sarandos, Co-CEO of Netflix, said in a statement. “Once he joined Netflix, I saw up close how his dedication to quality filmmaking, rigor around dealmaking and strategy, and collaborative spirit elevated our film business. I’m grateful to Dan for everything he’s done for Netflix films.”

Lin joined Netflix in February 2024 , replacing longtime film chief Scott Stuber. He came over from his own production house, Rideback, which built the “LEGO” film franchise, Stephen King’s popular “It” adaptations, and the “Sherlock Holmes” movies. During his time at the streamer, Lin greenlit and acquired over 85 movies, including “Apex,” “Emilia Pérez,” and “Train Dreams,” plus the upcoming titles “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” and Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew.”

As IndieWire noted earlier this year , “One of Lin’s hallmarks since taking over has been to organize his film team leaders based on genre , so individual executives are focused on producing 3-4 films a year each within distinct genres like comedy, drama, horror, sci-fi, etc.,” and it’s unclear if the streamer will continue with those distinctions as it continue to re-organize its business.

Though he did champion some ambitious foreign films and art house indies that were awards darlings, Lin had a reputation as being more interested in commercial fare rather than auteur-driven films than his predecessor Stuber. Some of his hits have included “Happy Gilmore 2,” “Frankenstein,” “The Perfect Neighbor,” “War Machine,” “The Rip,” “People We Meet on Vacation,” and “Remarkably Bright Creatures.” And though it originated as a Sony Animation film, he was at the helm when Netflix’s biggest title of all time came out, “KPop Demon Hunters.”

And yet Netflix across the board, not just on the film side, has struggled with engagement as it tries to compete with the likes of YouTube for total hours spent viewing. Lin’s approach has been to soften its position on theatrical, starting this weekend with reporting box office data for “La Bola Negra” for the first time in Netflix’s history, and it hopes to reach an even larger audience when next year it releases Gerwig’s “Narnia” in wide release with a healthy theatrical exclusive window before it premieres on Netflix.

Prior to founding Rideback, Dan served as SVP of Production for Warner Bros. Pictures between 1999 to 2007, overseeing production and development on titles such as “The Departed.”

Variety first reported the news of Lin’s exit.
excerpt_original: After less than three years at the streamer, Lin is the latest high-powered exec to exit Netflix as it reorganizes its org chart and cuts around 1,000 jobs in the process.
